div.head: IV Eg 2.1
div.ab: ⁊ ic wille, þæt woruldgerihta mid Denum standan be swa godum lagum, swa hy betste geceosan mægen.
⁊ ic wille, þæt woruldgerihta mid Denum standan be swa godum lagum, swa hy betste geceosan mægen.
Cupio ętiam cum Danis stare et uigere iustitiam et equitatem legumque bonarum et adinuentionem,
⁊ ic wille þæt woruldgerihta mid Denum standan be swa godum lagum, swa hy betste geceosan mægen.
Und ich will, dass weltliche Rechte bei den Dänen [Nordleuten] gemäss so guter Verfassung bestehen sollen, wie sie als beste auswählen können.
And I will that secular rights among the Danes [Northmen] stand according to as good laws as they can best choose.
And it is my will that the rights of the laity be maintained among the Danes in accordance with the best constitution which they can determine upon.
And it is my will that secular rights be in force among the Danes according to as good laws as they can best decide on.

note.seg: Vgl. Gl Partikularrecht 5. a; dieses wahrte auch Hu 6, 1. Kirchenrecht und das Gebot 2, 2ff. gelten dagegen auch für Denalagu
Cf. Gl Partikularrecht 5. a; this was also upheld by Hu 6, 1. Church law and the ordinance 2, 2ff., on the other hand, apply to the Denalagu as well
aequitas des Übersetzers ist nur Stilanhängsel, bed. nicht etwa technisch ‘Billigkeit (s. d. Gl 1. 3) im Ggs. zu strengem Recht’; vgl. Iudex 2
The translator's aequitas is merely a stylistic appendage; it does not, say, mean technically ‘equity (see that word in Gl 1. 3) as opposed to strict law’; cf. Iudex 2

Unter Dänen (s. d. Gl 8. 12ff.) sind Norweger mitverstanden; das Wort bed. ‘Anglo-Skandinaven’, genauer hier: das Rechtsgebiet der Denalagu. Hier wird Northumbrien zuerst ins Bereich auch weltlicher (kirchlich s. o. S. 124, 10) Gesetzgebung des Staates England gezogen; im Ggs. zur internationalen Rechtsgrundlage von II Ew 5, 2⁸.—Dass man aber nicht etwa folgere, die Dänen hätten hiermit persönliches Recht frei wählen dürfen, warnt mit Recht Savigny Gesch. Röm. Rechts im MA. III 654; vgl. Gl Denalagu 1b. Auch möcht ich nicht mit Björkman (Scandin. loanwords 4) hierin den Beweis sehen, dass die Dänen noch als Fremde beim Englischen Volke galten; in der Denalagu wohnten Hunderttausende rein Englischen Blutes; und ausserhalb waren manche Dänen angesiedelt, denen Englische Obrigkeit Englisches Recht sprach.—Die Selbstverwaltung belohnt die Dänen für deren Treue gegenüber Eadgar, auch laut 12. 13, 1. 14, 1f. Vielleicht leitete mancher Südengländer diese Tatsache her (statt von der Ohnmacht der Englischen Zentralregierung) von der Eadgar zur Last gelegten Vorliebe für fremde Sitte, worüber vgl. Plummer Saxon chron. II 153.—Selbst dieses Eine Reichsgesetz 3—11 ist im nördlichsten England insofern nicht Wirklichkeit geworden, als dort kein Hundred bestand

Danes (see that word in Gl 8. 12ff.) is understood to include Norwegians; the word means ‘Anglo-Scandinavians’, more precisely here: the legal area of the Denalagu. Here Northumbria is for the first time drawn into the sphere of the secular legislation, too, of the English state (for ecclesiastical legislation see above p. 124, 10); in contrast to the international legal basis of II Ew 5, 2⁸.—Savigny Gesch. Röm. Rechts im MA. III 654 rightly warns against inferring that the Danes were hereby allowed to choose their personal law freely; cf. Gl Denalagu 1b. Nor would I see in this, with Björkman (Scandin. loanwords 4), proof that the Danes were still regarded as foreigners by the English people; hundreds of thousands of people of purely English blood lived in the Denalagu; and outside it many Danes were settled to whom English authorities administered English law.—The self-government rewards the Danes for their loyalty to Eadgar, as also stated in 12. 13, 1. 14, 1f. Perhaps many a southern Englishman attributed this fact (instead of to the weakness of the English central government) to the predilection for foreign custom with which Eadgar was charged, on which cf. Plummer Saxon chron. II 153.—Even this single law for the whole realm, 3—11, did not become reality in the northernmost part of England, insofar as no hundred existed there

Schmid übersetzt ‘Gesetz’ auch 12. 13, 1, wo ebenfalls Plural steht. Allein hierfür sagt Eadgar dom, ræd. Erst im 11. Jh. (Ann. Agsax. a. 1086; Bibel-Übs. Levit. 26, 46) muss lagu ‘Gesetz’ heissen; vorher kann das Wort an zahlreichen Stellen zwar so, vielleicht aber ‘Rechtsordnung’ verstanden werden. Und zwar braucht Eg das Wort nur erst für das Recht der Dänen; Steenstrup Danelag 23f.

Schmid translates ‘law’, also at 12. 13, 1, where there is likewise a plural. But for this Eadgar says dom, ræd. Only in the 11th cent. (Ann. Agsax. a. 1086; Bible transl. Levit. 26, 46) must lagu mean ‘law’; before that the word can indeed be understood thus in numerous passages, but perhaps also as ‘legal order’. And indeed Eg as yet uses the word only for the law of the Danes; Steenstrup Danelag 23f.

lagum, see BT. p. 615, s.v. lagu and cf. Norse lög. Liebermann points out that Edgar uses this word only in referring to the constitution of the Danes (cf. cap. 12). In his laws it occurs only in the plural (as in Norse). It may be noted that in Norse it is a neuter pl. but in Æthelred and subsequent laws it appears as a fem. sing. The earlier meanings of the word would seem to be (1) legal conditions affecting a person or community (rights, privileges etc.) similar to gerihta; (2) the area within which such conditions were in force, e.g. Denelagu, Gulathingslög. In the eleventh century the word acquired its modern significance through the transitional meaning ‘regulations’ (affecting the condition of a person or community), cf. the phrase setja lög (originally leggja), meaning probably ‘to fix or determine the conditions of.’ At this time also it seems to have come into general use throughout the country (cf. Sax. Chr. D, ann. 1018 ad fin.), whereas in the tenth century it is used (like eorl and here in the political sense) only with reference to the Scandinavian districts.
Here and again in cap. 12 below autonomy is specially conceded to the Danes with the reservations expressed in caps. 2, 2; 12, 1; 14, 2. It is not specified, however, within what area this autonomy was to apply, but the reference in cap. 15 to Oslac (who bears the title eorl) and to the here under his rule seems to indicate that his province (York and the districts dependent on it) is intended. The former (Danish) East Anglian kingdom was under the ealdorman Æthelwine who is coupled with the Mercian ealdorman Ælfhere. This would seem to indicate that this province was not meant to be included. On the other hand we should expect the N.E. Midlands—the district of the Five Boroughs—to be under Danish law since they have a separate code devoted to them in the next reign, viz. III Atr. Possibly this district may have been included in Oslac’s province.
